astra.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, I think, to some extent, I still believe that. But I would be careful about saying it doesn't matter. So, what we showed was that, for those vision tasks, the choice between convolution and self-attention was not necessarily what explained the performance gap. A lot of the gap came from the other design choices around them.

And I think that's still an important lesson, right? When we compare two architectures, we're often comparing two whole systems. One might have a better training recipe, or people have spent more effort tuning its components. So it's difficult to attribute the improvement to just the one thing that gives the architecture its name.

But that doesn't mean they'll be equivalent for every task or at every scale. Architecture can still matter for efficiency, for example. So, yeah, I still believe the broader point, that we should look carefully at all the components before deciding that one fundamental design is better.

sol.text:
Yeah, I think broadly I still believe that, but with some nuance. I don’t mean that architecture never matters. It matters a lot for things like computational efficiency, scalability, and how easily you can integrate different modalities. But if the question is purely whether a model can learn strong visual representations, then I think many of these architectures—convolution, attention, or combinations of them—can reach very similar performance when the training recipe and all the surrounding design choices are controlled carefully.

And actually, that was one of the main lessons for me from that work: we often attribute an improvement to one big architectural idea, but the gain may come from many smaller choices that changed at the same time—the normalization, activation, stage design, optimization, data augmentation, and so on. Transformers have a very clean and general design, which is especially convenient as systems become larger and more multimodal. So their dominance is not accidental. But I would still be cautious about concluding that self-attention itself is always the essential ingredient, or that convolution has somehow become fundamentally obsolete.

opus.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, I, I do, actually. Maybe even more so now than back then. Um, so the way I would put it is, architecture matters much less than people think, as long as you're in the regime where you have, enough data and enough compute and you've tuned the training recipe properly. Like, if you fix the data and you fix the compute budget, a lot of, reasonable architectures will land in, in pretty much the same place. And we've seen this again and again, right? Like convnets versus vision transformers, and then MLP-Mixer, and then state space models versus transformers in language — every time there's a new architecture, the initial gap, a lot of it turns out to be, recipe and, and data.

But, mm, I want to be careful, because I don't want to say architecture is, is totally irrelevant. I think what I'd say is, the, the semantic behavior of the model, like what it learns, what mistakes it makes, its, biases, that's almost entirely determined by the data. We actually have some work on this, where you train very different architectures on the same data and, the, the errors they make are remarkably similar. So in that sense, the data is, is the, the real content of the model.

Where architecture still matters is more on the, the systems side. Like, how efficiently can you train it, how well does it map to the hardware, what's the, the memory cost at long context, how does it scale. Those are real differences, and, and they're not small. But they're, they're efficiency questions, not, "does this model understand the world better" questions. Yeah. So I would say, the, the field has maybe over-invested in architecture search and, under-invested in understanding data. Mm-hmm.

grok.text:
Yeah. So, I think, in many ways, yes. I still believe the main takeaway, which is that the gap people were seeing was not really because convolution is inherently worse than self-attention. If you modernize the other design components, the macro architecture, the training recipe, the scaling, you can get convnets to a very similar level as strong vision transformers, at least on a lot of the vision tasks we were looking at.

At the same time, I wouldn't go as far as to say it doesn't matter at all. There are still differences. Convolution has this built-in locality and translation equivariance, which can help when you have less data, or for certain dense prediction tasks. Self-attention is more flexible for long-range interactions. They also have different computational properties, like how they scale with resolution. And that work was in vision. If you go to language, or some other modalities, transformers have been much more dominant, in part because the inductive bias of convolution is less natural there.

So I would put it this way: the architecture family matters less than people thought at the time, but the details still matter, and depending on the problem, one might still have an edge. The more lasting message for me is that we should be careful not to attribute a performance gap to the most salient difference, attention versus convolution, when a lot of it is actually these other design choices. When we look at today's AI systems, a lot of the progress is from getting many of those components right together.

gemini.text:
Yeah, so I think, uh, yes and no. 

I think on one hand, if you look at, uh, pure computer vision tasks—like visual recognition, ImageNet classification, object detection, segmentation—I think it is still true. Modern convnets like ConvNeXt are still very competitive with vision transformers, and in many practical scenarios, they are faster, more memory-efficient, and easier to train and deploy. 

But on the other hand, if we look at the broader landscape of AI today, especially with the rise of foundation models, large language models, and multimodal systems, uh, transformers have a clear advantage. And that advantage is mainly about generality and universality. With transformers, you can tokenize everything—text, images, audio, video—and train them within a single unified architecture. And also, the entire industry has optimized the hardware and software infrastructure around transformers. 

So if you ask whether the core inductive bias—like convolution versus self-attention—fundamentally dictates performance on vision, I still believe it doesn't matter as much as people thought. But if you look at where AI is heading as a whole, the unified nature of transformers makes them much more dominant today.

kimi.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, that's a, that's a great question. So I think, to a large extent, I still believe it's true, especially for pure vision tasks. If you look at tasks like classification, detection, segmentation, a well-designed convnet with the right training recipe is still very competitive. And I think there has been follow-up work from other groups, showing that even at a very large compute scale, convnets can still match vision transformers. So the core message of the paper, I think, still holds, that a lot of the, the perceived gap back then was really due to training recipes and, like, seemingly small design details, and not due to the fundamental difference between, you know, convolution and self-attention.

But at the same time, I think the field has, has changed a lot since 2021, right? So the question people care about has kind of shifted, from which architecture is the best for vision, to how do you build a general foundation model that can handle language, vision, everything together. And there, I think the transformer has clearly won. But I would argue it's not necessarily because self-attention is inherently superior, but more because of this, like, positive feedback loop. Everybody is using transformers, so all the software, the kernels, the hardware, the community know-how, everything is optimized for transformers. And that makes it really hard for any alternative architecture to compete, even if it's, like, fundamentally just as good.

So the lesson I take from it is that the, the choice of the core operation matters less than people tend to think, and things like the training recipe, the data, the scale, matter a lot more. But the, the ecosystem effect is also very real, so today, if you ask me what architecture you should use, I would probably still say transformer, just because everything around it is so much more mature. Yeah.

So I think most of the, the gain we saw actually, came from the training recipe, the data, the, the augmentation, the optimization, like, all these things. So, uh, it's more like, uh, the modeling, uh, the, the, the model architecture is one component, but it's, it's not the most important component. So that part, I think I still believe.

But, um, I think, uh, there are some things that, uh, maybe I, I would say a little differently now. So, so the first thing is, uh, transformers, I think they have a, a big advantage in terms of, uh, generality, right? So, so it's not just about vision anymore. So now everybody wants to have one architecture that can do language, vision, audio, uh, everything, and, uh, the transformer is, is very natural for that, because it just takes in a sequence of tokens. It doesn't really care, uh, whether the token comes from an image patch or a, a word or, or something else. And for, for a convnet, that's, that's a little harder, because the convolution has this built-in, uh, assumption about locality, about the, the, the grid structure. So, so for, for something like a multimodal LLM, I think, uh, the transformer is, is just the more convenient choice.

And the second thing is, uh, I think there's, there's a lot of, uh, ecosystem effects, right? So, so the whole, uh, community, the whole industry, uh, has been optimizing for transformers for, for many years now. Uh, the, the hardware, the kernels, uh, like flash attention, uh, the, the, the, the distributed training infrastructure, everything. So even if, uh, in principle, a convnet could get the, the same performance, uh, in practice, uh, it's, it's a lot easier to, to just use a transformer, because everything is built around it. So, so I think this is, uh, this is a kind of, like, self-reinforcing thing.

So, yeah, so, so my, my current view is, uh, I think the, the inherent, uh, inductive bias, the, the, the difference between convolution and attention, it, it, it doesn't matter that much. Uh, what, what really matters is the, the data and the, the training and, and scaling. But, uh, at the same time, uh, I think the transformer won not really because of, of attention itself being magical, but because it's, it's, it's more flexible, it's more general, and, uh, everybody is using it. Uh, and, and I think that, that's, that's a, uh, that's a fine reason. Yeah.
